Double scoring: agreement before rater inference

Source: vignettes/articles/application-double-scoring.Rmd
application-double-scoring.Rmd

A team has an original score and a second score for each selected answer. Its first question is where the two scores disagree. That question can be answered before fitting a measurement model. Estimating which individual rater is more severe needs additional information about who scored each answer.

IEA scoring-reliability files are one possible application. The TIMSS 2019 international database guide, Chapter 2 describes original scores, second scores and agreement codes. This example uses invented observations only, with score-code families described in that guide. It contains no IEA records, released items or copied result tables. It uses base R; mfrmr is useful later if the study question and rating design support a model.

Keep score agreement and code agreement distinct

In this coding scheme, 10 and 11 both award one point but describe different response codes. Codes in 70:79 award zero points. An omitted answer (99), an answer not reached (96) and a structurally absent observation (NA) remain distinct in the input. For this descriptive comparison, a pair enters the denominator only when both observations map to valid scores. This is not an achievement-scoring rule or a reproduction of an official IEA summary.

Show R code: make the small example and map scores 
paired <- data.frame(
  Answer = paste0("answer", 1:12),
  Item = rep(c("item_a", "item_b"), each = 6),
  OriginalCode = c(10, 10, 70, 20, 99, NA, 70, 10, 20, 96, 10, 70),
  SecondCode   = c(10, 11, 10, 20, 10, 70, 79, 70, 20, 10, 99, 70)
)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(paired[c("Answer", "Item")]))

# This mapping is for the stated coding scheme, not every IEA study/cycle.
score_codes <- c(70:79, 10:19, 20:29)
score_points <- rep(0:2, each = 10)
observed_codes <- c(paired$OriginalCode, paired$SecondCode)
stopifnot(all(is.na(observed_codes) |
              observed_codes %in% c(score_codes, 96, 99)))
paired$OriginalScore <- score_points[match(paired$OriginalCode, score_codes)]
paired$SecondScore <- score_points[match(paired$SecondCode, score_codes)]
paired$ValidPair <- !is.na(paired$OriginalScore) & !is.na(paired$SecondScore)
Invented paired observations; raw codes are retained.
Answer Item OriginalCode SecondCode OriginalScore SecondScore ValidPair
answer1 item_a 10 10 1 1 TRUE
answer2 item_a 10 11 1 1 TRUE
answer3 item_a 70 10 0 1 TRUE
answer4 item_a 20 20 2 2 TRUE
answer5 item_a 99 10 NA 1 FALSE
answer6 item_a NA 70 NA 0 FALSE
answer7 item_b 70 79 0 0 TRUE
answer8 item_b 10 70 1 0 TRUE
answer9 item_b 20 20 2 2 TRUE
answer10 item_b 96 10 NA 1 FALSE
answer11 item_b 10 99 1 NA FALSE
answer12 item_b 70 70 0 0 TRUE

Report the denominator alongside agreement

Show R code: summarize each item 
agreement <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(paired, paired$Item), function(x) {
  valid <- x[x$ValidPair, , drop = FALSE]
  n <- nrow(valid)
  code_equal <- sum(valid$OriginalCode == valid$SecondCode)
  score_equal <- sum(valid$OriginalScore == valid$SecondScore)
  data.frame(
    Item = x$Item[1], Pairs = nrow(x), ValidPairs = n,
    ExcludedPairs = nrow(x) - n,
    CodeAgreement = if (n > 0) code_equal / n else NA_real_,
    ScoreAgreement = if (n > 0) score_equal / n else NA_real_,
    SecondHigher = sum(valid$SecondScore > valid$OriginalScore),
    SecondLower = sum(valid$SecondScore < valid$OriginalScore)
  )
}))
rownames(agreement) <- NULL
Item Pairs ValidPairs ExcludedPairs CodeAgreement ScoreAgreement SecondHigher SecondLower
item_a 6 4 2 0.5 0.75 1 0
item_b 6 4 2 0.5 0.75 0 1

Both items have four valid pairs out of six. Three of the four pairs agree in points, while two agree in the full response code. One disagreement increases the second score in item A; one decreases it in item B. Inspect those answers and the scoring instructions before attributing the differences to a rater.

The original score is a comparison, not an independently established correct answer. High agreement can coexist with shared scoring errors. When combining items, an unweighted mean of item agreement and agreement pooled over all pairs answer different questions if the denominators differ.

Decide whether a rater model answers the next question

Question Information needed
Which answers or score categories need review? Paired scores, their raw codes and explicit missingness/denominators. The table above is sufficient for a descriptive starting point.
Is original scoring systematically different from second scoring? A defined scoring-role contrast, assignment information and treatment of the shared answer being scored twice. Roles are not individual identities.
Which individual rater has higher severity? Actual rater IDs, enough linked assignments, supported categories and an identifiable measurement specification.
What would happen with a different number of raters? A justified generalization universe and an appropriate G-Study design; paired agreement alone does not identify that projection.

The inspected TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 public schema and Japanese ASR file do not contain individual scorer IDs. IDGRADER identifies the grade, not the grader. Labelling every original score as one person and every second score as another would therefore change the meaning of the data. The files may still inform agreement analysis and realistic exposure patterns.

For a design with actual rater identities, continue with the rating agreement guide and model-choice guide. Different maximum item scores and dependence between repeated scores require their own model decisions. No model fit or rater-severity result is claimed for the invented table above.

Apply the idea to an external file

Obtain data and the matching codebook from the official TIMSS 2019 database. Check the IEA usage terms before use or sharing. Keep downloaded data outside a published repository. Prepare the same paired-score columns locally, retaining the original codes, item-specific score ranges, IDs and reasons for exclusion. Confirm the coding scheme for that study and cycle before adapting the mapping above.

To reproduce an official statistic, also match its item selection, handling of omissions, weighting and aggregation. The TIMSS 2019 within-country reliability appendix is a reference for the reporting definition. Survey inference from a double-scored subset additionally needs its sampling/selection justification. An analysis of official plausible values is a separate task; it need not be added to this agreement workflow.
